title: web.dev (Google), Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
text:
## Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)

LCP reports the render time of the largest image, text block, or video visible in the viewport, relative to when the user first navigated to the page.

## Thresholds

Good: 2.5 seconds or less. Needs Improvement: between 2.5 and 4.0 seconds. Poor: greater than 4.0 seconds. Thresholds are measured at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop devices.

## Qualifying elements

LCP candidates include: img elements (using first frame presentation time for animated content), image elements inside svg, video elements (poster image or first frame, whichever is earlier), elements with background images loaded via the url() function, and block-level elements containing text nodes or inline text children.

## Timing components

LCP includes any unload time from the previous page, connection set up time, redirect time, and other Time To First Byte (TTFB) delays, which can create field versus lab measurement differences. LCP can be broken into four subparts: time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load time, and element render delay. The browser stops reporting new LCP entries as soon as the user interacts with the page via a tap, scroll, or keypress, so you should only report the most recently dispatched entry to analytics.

title: web.dev (Google), Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
text:
## Interaction to Next Paint (INP)

INP is a metric that assesses a page's overall responsiveness to user interactions by observing the latency of all click, tap, and keyboard interactions that occur throughout the lifespan of a user's visit to a page. The final INP value is the longest interaction observed, ignoring outliers.

## Measured interaction types

Only three categories qualify: clicking with a mouse, tapping on a device with a touchscreen, and pressing a key on either a physical or onscreen keyboard. Scrolling, hovering, and zooming are explicitly excluded.

## Thresholds (75th percentile)

Good: below or at 200 milliseconds. Needs Improvement: above 200 milliseconds and below or at 500 milliseconds. Poor: above 500 milliseconds.

## Three phases of interaction latency

1. Input delay: the time before event handlers begin executing, often caused by blocking tasks on the main thread. 2. Processing duration: the time for all event handler callbacks to run to completion. 3. Presentation delay: the time after callbacks finish until the next frame is painted on screen. INP is measured from user input initiation until the next frame renders. For pages with many interactions, the calculation ignores the single highest interaction per roughly 50 interactions to discount outliers.

title: web.dev (Google), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
text:
## Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)

CLS is a measure of the largest burst of layout shift scores for every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the entire lifecycle of a page. A layout shift happens when a visible element changes position between two rendered frames.

## Layout shift score formula

layout shift score = impact fraction x distance fraction. The impact fraction measures how the unstable elements affect the viewport area between two frames, expressed as a fraction of the total viewport. The distance fraction is the greatest horizontal or vertical distance any unstable element has moved, divided by the viewport's largest dimension (width or height).

## Thresholds

Good: 0.1 or less. Needs improvement: between 0.1 and 0.25. Poor: greater than 0.25. Measured at the 75th percentile across mobile and desktop.

## Session windows

Layout shifts are grouped into session windows: one or more individual layout shifts occurring in rapid succession with less than 1 second between each shift and a maximum of 5 seconds for the total window duration. CLS reports the largest burst.

## Common causes and prevention

Primary causes: images and videos without dimensions, ads and embeds without reserved space, dynamically injected content, and web fonts causing FOIT/FOUT. Fixes: always include width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) on media, reserve space for dynamic content, prefer CSS transforms over properties that trigger layout, and never insert content above existing content except in response to a user interaction.

title: react.dev (official React docs), Rules of Hooks
text:
## Rules of Hooks

Functions whose names start with use are called Hooks. Hooks have two rules.

## Rule 1: Only call Hooks at the top level

Don't call Hooks inside loops, conditions, nested functions, or try / catch / finally blocks. Always use Hooks at the top level of your React function, before any early returns. Hooks can only be called while React is rendering a function component.

Valid: at the top level of a function component body, and at the top level of a custom Hook body.

Invalid: inside a condition or loop, after a conditional return statement, in event handlers, in class components, inside functions passed to useMemo, useReducer, or useEffect, and inside try / catch / finally blocks.

## Rule 2: Only call Hooks from React functions

Don't call Hooks from regular JavaScript functions. Valid callers are React function components and custom Hooks. Following this rule ensures that all stateful logic in a component is clearly visible from its source code.

## Why these rules exist

React relies on the call order of Hooks being identical on every render to associate each Hook call with its internal state. Conditionally calling a Hook changes that order and corrupts the state mapping. Use the eslint-plugin-react-hooks plugin to catch these mistakes automatically.

title: react.dev (official React docs), Rendering Lists and Keys
text:
## Rendering lists with keys

Keys tell React which array item each component corresponds to, so React can match items between renders. This matters when items can move, get inserted, or get deleted. A well chosen key gives React more information than a position in the array, so even when the position changes because of reordering, the key lets React identify the item throughout its lifetime.

## Rules of keys

Keys must be unique among siblings (the same key may be reused across different arrays). Keys must not change, or they defeat their purpose, so do not generate them while rendering. Components do not receive key as a prop; if a component needs an id, pass it separately, for example key={id} userId={id}.

## Where to get a key

Data from a database: use the database keys or ids, which are unique by nature. Locally generated data: use an incrementing counter, crypto.randomUUID(), or a package like uuid when the item is created.

## Anti-patterns

Don't use an item's index in the array as its key. Index as a key often leads to subtle and confusing bugs because the render order changes over time when an item is inserted, deleted, or the array is reordered. Do not generate keys on the fly, for example key={Math.random()}. This causes keys to never match between renders, so all components and DOM are recreated every time, which is slow and loses any user input inside the list items. Instead use a stable id based on the data.

title: react.dev (official React docs), You Might Not Need an Effect
text:
## You might not need an Effect

Effects are an escape hatch for synchronizing with external systems. You do not need Effects in two common cases: transforming data for rendering, and handling user events.

## Don't use Effects to transform data for rendering

If you want to filter, transform, or compute data before display, do it during rendering instead of storing it in state and syncing with an Effect. This avoids extra render passes and is simpler and less error prone. For expensive calculations wrap them in useMemo.

## Don't use Effects to handle user events

Effects don't know what the user did, event handlers do. Logic that should run because the user performed an action belongs in an event handler, not an Effect.

## Common removable patterns

Resetting state when a prop changes: pass a different key to the component so React treats it as a new instance and resets state automatically, rather than resetting in an Effect. Adjusting some state when a prop changes: update state during rendering with a stored previous value, or better, restructure so the value is derived instead of stored. Sharing logic between event handlers: extract a shared function, don't put it in an Effect. Chains of Effects that trigger each other are an anti-pattern: calculate everything you can in the event handler instead.

## When Effects ARE appropriate

Running code because the component was displayed (such as sending an analytics event, or fetching data). For data fetching, guard against race conditions with a cleanup flag: set let ignore = false, ignore stale responses inside the promise, and set ignore = true in the cleanup function.

## Decision framework

Ask why the code needs to run. Because the component was displayed, use an Effect. Because the user performed an action, use an event handler. Because you need to compute a value, calculate during rendering or use useMemo.

title: web.dev (Google), Optimize Interaction to Next Paint
text:
## Optimize INP

Websites should strive to have an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, measured at the 75th percentile across mobile and desktop. Interactions have three components to optimize: input delay, processing duration, and presentation delay.

## Reduce input delay

Minimize blocking activity on the main thread during page load. Long tasks caused by script parsing, compilation, and evaluation prevent the browser from responding to user input. A long task is any task that occupies the main thread for 50 milliseconds or more.

## Optimize event callbacks

Yield to the main thread: break up complex callback work into separate tasks (for example with setTimeout, or the scheduler.yield API) so a single long task does not block other interactions. Yield strategically for rendering: defer non-critical work until after the visual update is queued, for example by running background work like saving or spell checking after a requestAnimationFrame plus setTimeout so render-critical updates paint first. Avoid layout thrashing: layout thrashing occurs when you update styles in JavaScript and then read them back in the same task, forcing synchronous (forced) layout.

## Reduce presentation delay

Minimize DOM size, because a large DOM increases rendering cost for both initial load and interaction responses. Use the CSS content-visibility property to lazily render off-screen elements. Be aware that JavaScript-rendered HTML does not benefit from the browser's streaming HTML parser, so heavy client-side rendering can delay the next paint.

title: W3C WAI, Understanding WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
text:
## SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA

The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for large text, incidental text, and logotypes.

## Large text

Large-scale text and images of large-scale text have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. Large text is defined as at least 18 point, or 14 point bold, or a font size that yields an equivalent size for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) fonts. In pixels, 14pt and 18pt are approximately 18.5px and 24px.

## Exceptions

No contrast requirement applies to: text or images of text that are part of an inactive (disabled) user interface component, pure decoration, text that is not visible to anyone, and text that is part of a logo or brand name.

## Level AAA (SC 1.4.6 Contrast Enhanced)

The enhanced ratio is 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text, compensating for the loss in contrast sensitivity of users with roughly 20/80 vision. The 4.5:1 AA ratio itself was chosen to compensate for roughly 20/40 vision, a common level of low vision.

title: W3C WAI, Understanding WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance
text:
## SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, Level AAA (new in WCAG 2.2)

When the keyboard focus indicator is visible, it must meet two requirements. Minimum area: the focus indicator must be at least as large as the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the unfocused component. A solid 2px outline is the simplest way to comply, though other shapes qualify if they meet the area calculation. Contrast: there must be a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states. This measures the change of contrast between the two states, not adjacent contrast.

## Distinction from Non-text Contrast

SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast measures adjacent contrast between the indicator and neighboring colors in a single state. An indicator can pass Focus Appearance while failing Non-text Contrast, or the reverse.

## Related new WCAG 2.2 criteria

SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA: when a component receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden by author-created content. SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA: pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exceptions for spacing, inline targets, and equivalents. SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA) requires that the keyboard focus indicator be visible at all.

title: W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions
text:
## Accessible names and descriptions

An accessible name is a short string, typically 1 to 3 words, that authors associate with an element to give assistive technology users a label. It conveys the element's purpose and distinguishes it from other elements.

## Cardinal rules

Test thoroughly with assistive technologies, because some patterns produce inconsistent browser results. Prefer visible text: when the interface already includes visible text that could serve as the name, using it simplifies maintenance, prevents bugs, and reduces translation work. Prefer native techniques: use label, legend, and caption before ARIA attributes. Avoid browser fallback: do not rely on title or placeholder, which generate low-quality names. Compose brief, useful names and place distinguishing words first.

## Naming precedence order

Browsers compute the accessible name in this priority order: 1. aria-labelledby (highest priority; can reference multiple elements and hidden content). 2. aria-label (explicit string). 3. Native HTML naming: label, legend, caption, alt. 4. Child content (for buttons, links, headings). 5. Fallback attributes title, then placeholder (lowest priority).

## Composition guidelines

Convey function not form (use Close, not X). Place the important distinguishing words first, especially verbs for actions. Keep names concise. Never include the role name in the accessible name. Ensure names are unique across elements that share the same role. A native label element also enlarges the clickable hit area of the control it labels.

title: MDN Web Docs, HTML Content Categories (Semantic HTML)
text:
## HTML content categories

HTML elements are grouped into content categories that define their permitted content models. Understanding them is the foundation of writing valid semantic HTML.

## The main categories

Metadata content: modifies presentation or links to other documents, lives in the head: base, link, meta, noscript, script, style, template, title. Flow content: the broadest category, most elements that go in the body. Sectioning content: creates sections in the document outline and scopes header and footer: article, aside, nav, section. Heading content: defines section titles: h1 to h6 and hgroup (header is not itself heading content but may contain it). Phrasing content: text and inline markup within paragraphs: span, em, strong, a, img, input, label, textarea, and more. Embedded content: imports external resources: audio, canvas, embed, iframe, img, math, object, picture, svg, video. Interactive content: designed for user interaction, always interactive are button, details, embed, iframe, label, select, textarea, and conditionally interactive are a (with href), audio and video (with controls), input (not hidden).

## Additional categories

Palpable content: rendered and substantive, not empty or hidden. Form-associated content: elements with a form owner, including listed, submittable, resettable, and labelable subgroups. Script-supporting elements: script and template, which support scripts rather than rendered output. Some elements use a transparent content model (such as ins and del), adopting the permitted content of their parent.

title: MDN Web Docs, Keyboard-navigable JavaScript widgets
text:
## Making custom widgets keyboard navigable

The tabindex attribute controls keyboard focus. tabindex not present: follows platform convention (links and form controls are focusable and in the tab order). tabindex="-1": focusable by element.focus() only, not reachable by pressing Tab; used for programmatically managed focus. tabindex="0": makes a non-interactive element focusable and inserts it into the natural tab order based on document position. A positive tabindex (for example 33) is an anti-pattern: it puts the element before the default interactive elements, forcing authors to set and maintain tabindex on every focusable element on the page.

## Roving tabindex

For composite widgets (menus, tab lists, grids, tree views), give the container or active child tabindex="0" and all other children tabindex="-1". On arrow-key press, call element.focus() on the new element, set its tabindex to 0, and set the previously focused element's tabindex to -1. This keeps a single tab stop for the whole widget and returns focus to the last active item.

## aria-activedescendant alternative

Bind a single handler to the container, track virtual focus with aria-activedescendant, and update styling to indicate focus.

## Essential guidelines

Do not dispatch the focus event to move focus; call element.focus() instead, and listen to focus and blur to track changes. Use document.activeElement to read the focused element. Ensure keyboard and mouse handlers produce identical results. Always show a focus indicator: style the outline property and prefer the :focus-visible pseudo-class so the ring appears for keyboard users without being removed for everyone.

title: MDN Web Docs, Basic concepts of flexbox
text:
## Flexbox basic concepts

Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout model that distributes space along a single axis (a row or a column) with rich alignment control. For two-dimensional layouts controlling rows and columns together, use CSS Grid.

## The two axes

The main axis is set by flex-direction: row, row-reverse, column, or column-reverse. The cross axis runs perpendicular to the main axis.

## Container and items

display: flex creates a block-level flex container; display: inline-flex an inline one. Direct children become flex items. Defaults: items lay out in a row, start at the main-axis start edge, do not grow (flex-grow: 0), can shrink (flex-shrink: 1), stretch to fill the cross axis (align-items: stretch), use flex-basis: auto, and stay on a single line (flex-wrap: nowrap).

## Item sizing

flex-basis: the item's size before free space is distributed. flex-grow: how much an item grows into available space, proportionally (0 means no growth). flex-shrink: how much an item shrinks when space is tight. The flex shorthand combines all three: flex: 1 means 1 1 0, flex: auto means 1 1 auto, flex: none means 0 0 auto (fully inflexible), and the initial value is 0 1 auto.

## Alignment

justify-content aligns items on the main axis: flex-start, flex-end, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly. align-items aligns on the cross axis: stretch, flex-start, flex-end, center, baseline. align-self overrides align-items for a single item. Flexbox is ideal for navigation bars, centering content, and distributing space between component-level items.

title: MDN Web Docs, Basic concepts of CSS grid layout
text:
## CSS Grid basic concepts

display: grid (or inline-grid) creates a grid container; its direct children become grid items. Grid is two-dimensional, controlling rows and columns simultaneously, which makes it well suited to page-level layouts, whereas flexbox is better for one-dimensional component layouts.

## Tracks and the fr unit

Grid tracks (columns and rows) are defined with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. The fr unit represents a fraction of the available space: grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr makes three equal columns, and 2fr 1fr 1fr gives the first column twice the share. You can mix absolute and flexible sizes, for example 500px 1fr 2fr.

## repeat() and minmax()

repeat(3, 1fr) is shorthand for 1fr 1fr 1fr, and repeat() also handles patterns like 20px repeat(6, 1fr) 20px. minmax(min, max) sets a track's minimum and maximum size, for example grid-auto-rows: minmax(100px, auto) makes implicit rows at least 100px tall but able to grow.

## Lines, gaps, cells, areas

Grid lines are numbered from 1; a 3-column grid has 4 column lines. Items can be positioned with grid-column and grid-row (for example grid-column: 1 / 4). Spacing between tracks is set with column-gap, row-gap, or the gap shorthand; gaps behave like transparent tracks and hold no content. A grid cell is one row by one column; a grid area spans multiple cells and must be rectangular.

## Explicit vs implicit grid

The explicit grid is defined by grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. Extra tracks created automatically when content overflows form the implicit grid, sized by grid-auto-rows and grid-auto-columns.

title: web.dev (Google), Performance budgets 101
text:
## Performance budgets

A performance budget is a set of limits imposed on metrics that affect site performance. It becomes the point of reference for making design, technology, and feature decisions, so teams can add features without silently degrading speed.

## Types of metrics

Quantity-based metrics track concrete assets: total page weight, HTTP request counts, maximum image sizes, web font limits, and script sizes including frameworks. Milestone timings measure user experience during load, such as First Contentful Paint (when initial content appears) and Time to Interactive (when the page reliably responds to input). Rule-based metrics use tools like Lighthouse to score a site against best-practice rules.

## Recommended starting baselines

For 3G networks on a standard mobile device: under 5 seconds Time to Interactive, and under 170 KB of critical-path resources (compressed and minified). These figures are based on real-world baseline devices and 3G speeds, reflecting that over half of internet traffic is on mobile networks.

## Enforcement

Integrate budget limits into the build with tools such as Webpack performance hints, bundlesize, and Lighthouse CI. When a budget is exceeded, teams either optimize existing features, remove assets, or block the new addition.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Hick's Law
text:
## Hick's Law

The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.

## Takeaways

1. Minimize choices when response times are critical to decrease decision time. 2. Break complex tasks into smaller steps to decrease cognitive load. 3. Avoid overwhelming users by highlighting recommended options. 4. Use progressive onboarding to minimize cognitive load for new users. 5. Be careful not to simplify to the point of abstraction.

## Origin

Also called the Hick-Hyman Law, from 1952 research by psychologists William Edmund Hick and Ray Hyman on how the number of available stimuli affects reaction time. The core finding: more choices lead to longer decision-making, because users must interpret and evaluate options they may not want.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Jakob's Law
text:
## Jakob's Law

Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

## Takeaways

1. Users transfer expectations they have built around one familiar product to another that appears similar. 2. By leveraging existing mental models, we create superior experiences in which users focus on their tasks rather than on learning new models. 3. When making changes, minimize discord by empowering users to continue using a familiar version for a limited time. Named after usability expert Jakob Nielsen.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Aesthetic-Usability Effect
text:
## Aesthetic-Usability Effect

Users often perceive aesthetically pleasing design as design that is more usable.

## Takeaways

1. An aesthetically pleasing design creates a positive response in people's brains and leads them to believe the design actually works better. 2. People are more tolerant of minor usability issues when the design of a product or service is aesthetically pleasing. 3. Visually pleasing design can mask usability problems and prevent issues from being discovered during usability testing. The practical caution: attractive prototypes can hide real problems, so do not let polish substitute for usability testing.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Miller's Law
text:
## Miller's Law

The average person can only keep 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory.

## Takeaways

1. Avoid using the magical number seven as justification for design constraints that are not truly necessary. 2. Breaking content into smaller chunks helps users process, comprehend, and retain information more easily. 3. Working memory capacity differs among individuals based on their existing knowledge and the situation. Chunking (for example grouping a phone number or organizing an interface into sections) is the practical application, as seen in simple remote-control layouts.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Doherty Threshold
text:
## Doherty Threshold

Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (less than 400 ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

## Takeaways

1. Provide system feedback within 400 ms to maintain user attention and boost productivity. 2. Leverage perceived performance to enhance response time and lessen the sense of delay. 3. Animation can visually occupy users during background processing or loading. 4. Progress bars make waiting periods more bearable, independent of their precision. 5. Intentionally adding delay can enhance perceived value and build user confidence, even when execution is much faster.

## Origin

From a 1982 IBM Systems Journal paper by Walter J. Doherty and Ahrvind J. Thadani, which established 400 milliseconds as the response-time standard, replacing the previous 2-second benchmark.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Law of Proximity (Gestalt)
text:
## Law of Proximity

Objects that are near, or proximate to each other, tend to be grouped together.

## Takeaways

1. Proximity helps to establish a relationship with nearby objects. 2. Elements in close proximity are perceived to share similar functionality or traits. 3. Proximity helps users understand and organize information faster and more efficiently. This Gestalt principle means whitespace and grouping, not boxes and borders, are often the strongest tools for showing which elements belong together in an interface.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)
text:
## Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)

When multiple similar objects are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be remembered.

## Takeaways

1. Make important information or key actions visually distinctive. 2. Use restraint when placing emphasis so elements do not compete with one another, and so salient items are not mistaken for ads. 3. Do not exclude those with color vision deficiency or low vision by relying exclusively on color to communicate contrast. 4. Carefully consider users with motion sensitivity when using motion to communicate contrast.

## Origin

Named after Hedwig von Restorff, whose 1933 research showed distinctive items in a homogeneous list are better remembered. This is the theoretical basis for a single, clearly dominant primary call to action per screen.

title: Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski), Tesler's Law (Conservation of Complexity)
text:
## Tesler's Law (Law of Conservation of Complexity)

For any system there is a certain amount of complexity which cannot be reduced.

## Takeaways

1. Every process contains irreducible complexity that must be managed by either the system or the user, rather than eliminated through design. 2. Designers should shift the burden of inherent complexity away from end users during design and development. 3. Products should accommodate real human behavior rather than assume perfect rationality. 4. Contextual guidance such as tooltips and help features should be readily available regardless of the interaction path. Named after Larry Tesler: the question is never whether complexity exists, but who absorbs it, the engineer or the user.

title: W3C Design Tokens Community Group, Design Tokens Format Module
text:
## Design tokens

A design token is information associated with a human readable name, at minimum a name/value pair, for example color-text-primary: #000000 or font-size-heading-level-1: 44px. Tokens are a methodology for expressing design decisions in a platform-agnostic way so they can be shared across disciplines, tools, and technologies.

## Structure

Every token requires a name (a case-sensitive JSON string that cannot begin with $ or contain the characters { } or period) and a value specified via the $value property. Optional properties: $type (categorizes the token, for example color, dimension, duration), $description (plain-text purpose), $deprecated, and $extensions (vendor metadata using reverse domain notation).

## Token types

Color, dimension (px or rem), fontFamily (a name or ordered array), fontWeight (1 to 1000 or predefined strings), duration (ms or s), cubicBezier (four numbers), and number (unitless).

## Composite types

Border, shadow, transition, strokeStyle, gradient, and typography combine multiple sub-values.

## Aliases and references

Tokens can reference other tokens. Curly-brace syntax like {colors.blue} always resolves to the $value of the target token. Circular references are prohibited and tools must detect and report them as errors. Aliases are what let a semantic token (color-text-primary) point at a primitive token (blue-900), the core of a themeable, single-source-of-truth token system.

title: spec.fm (Built by Buffer), The 8-Point Grid
text:
## The 8-point grid

Most popular screen sizes are divisible by 8 on at least one axis, usually both, which makes 8 a practical base unit for multi-platform design.

## Core principle

Use multiples of 8 to define the dimensions, padding, and margin of both block and inline elements. All spacing, sizing, and layout measurements follow 8-point increments (8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48).

## Hard grid vs soft grid

Hard grid: display an actual 8-point grid and align to it, using transparent spacer elements grouped with foreground content to track spacing (Material Design fits this approach). Soft grid: measure only the 8-point increments between individual elements without a visible grid, which is faster to iterate because the actual grid becomes irrelevant once the interface is coded.

## The 4-point subgrid

For text, combine the 8pt UI grid with a 4pt baseline grid. This keeps the math simple while giving enough options to fit a variety of text styles, and it establishes vertical rhythm and legibility for typography.

## Benefits

Automatic consistency across the UI, fewer spacing decisions (which accelerates design to code), and easy accommodation of responsive, multi-platform design.

title: Matthew Butterick, Practical Typography: Summary of Key Rules
text:
## Butterick's key typography rules

The four choices that most determine how body text looks are point size, line spacing, line length, and font choice.

## Specific measurements

Point size: 10 to 12 points in printed documents, 15 to 25 pixels on the web. Line spacing (line height): 120 to 145 percent of the point size. Line length: 45 to 90 characters including spaces.

## The single most effective improvement

The easiest and most visible improvement you can make to your typography is to use a professional font. Butterick advises avoiding goofy fonts, monospaced fonts, most free fonts, system fonts, Times New Roman, and Arial in favor of professionally designed typefaces. These few numeric rules (size, leading, measure) drive most of the legibility of an interface's reading experience and are the backbone of any typographic scale.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Design Systems 101
text:
## What a design system is

A design system is a complete set of standards intended to manage design at scale using reusable components and patterns. It exists because organizations must produce many products and pages consistently.

## Three core components

Style guide: implementation guidelines, visual references, and design principles for colors, typography, tone of voice, and interaction standards. Component library: reusable UI elements with names, descriptions, attributes, states, code snippets, and framework specifications. Pattern library: collections and groupings of UI elements such as layouts, templates, and content structures designed for reuse and adaptation.

## Benefits

Speed and scale (premade components replicate designs quickly), resource efficiency (teams focus on hard problems like information architecture rather than redrawing basic elements), a unified shared language across designers and developers, visual consistency across products and channels, and educational value for junior and new contributors.

## Drawbacks

A design system needs a dedicated team for continuous maintenance and evolution, time to train users on proper implementation, and it can face resistance from teams who see projects as one-offs. Three adoption approaches: adopt an existing system (lowest cost), adapt an existing system (moderate), or create a custom system (highest investment and control).

title: Adam Wathan and Steve Schoger (Refactoring UI), 7 Practical Tips for Cheating at Design
text:
## 7 practical tips for cheating at design

1. Use color and weight to create hierarchy instead of font size. Keep two to three text colors (dark for primary content, grey for secondary, lighter grey for ancillary) and two font weights (normal around 400 to 500, bold around 600 to 700).

2. Don't use grey text on colored backgrounds. Instead reduce contrast on colorful backgrounds either by reducing white text opacity so the background shows through, or by hand-picking a color based on the background's hue and adjusting saturation and lightness.

3. Offset shadows: add a vertical offset to a shadow instead of a large even blur, which simulates a light source from above and looks more natural.

4. Use fewer borders. For separation, prefer a box shadow, a different background color on adjacent elements, or simply more spacing, rather than adding a border.

5. Don't blow up small icons. Icons drawn at 16 to 24px never look professional at 3x or 4x size; enclose them in a shape with a background color instead.

6. Use accent borders. A colorful accent border on the side of an alert, an active nav item, or the top of a card makes an interface feel intentionally designed.

7. Design buttons by hierarchy, not semantics. Primary actions get a solid high-contrast background, secondary actions use an outline, and tertiary actions are styled like links. The theme throughout: emphasize the important and de-emphasize the rest, using color, weight, and spacing rather than raw talent.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Visual Hierarchy in UX: Definition
text:
## Visual hierarchy

Visual hierarchy is the organization of design elements on the page so that the eye is guided to consume each element in the order of intended importance. Clear hierarchy lets users know where to focus and makes a page easy to scan and act on; without it users face clutter and cannot tell where to look.

## Attributes that create hierarchy

Color and contrast: use contrast in value and saturation between an element and its context to direct attention (bright, saturated colors advance; muted tones recede); type contrast such as bold or italic reinforces it. What matters is the contrast, not the specific color. Scale: larger elements draw attention first; use no more than three size steps (small, medium, large) to keep relationships clear. Grouping (proximity and common regions): tight spacing between related items signals connection, more spacing separates groups, and containers, borders, or backgrounds explicitly define regions.

## The squint test

Blurring a design (the squint test) removes text detail and reveals whether size, contrast, and grouping actually produce the intended hierarchy.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Visual Design Glossary
text:
## Visual design glossary

Whitespace (negative space): the empty space between design elements used to achieve a balanced design, making it easier for users to scan and read. Contrast: the difference in visual properties, including color, brightness, or size, that makes an object distinguishable from its surroundings. Scale: using relative size to communicate importance and ranking within a composition. Proximity: design elements near each other are perceived as related, while elements spaced apart are perceived as belonging to separate groups. Grid: a structure of columns, gutters, and margins that provides the layout for elements on a page. Visual hierarchy: the organization of design elements so the eye is guided to consume each element in the order of intended importance. Visual balance: a satisfying arrangement or proportion of design elements, achieved through symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial distribution. Consistency: applying similar characteristics (layout, typography, color) across elements to establish coherence and predictability. Density: the concentration of visual elements in an area; high density reads as cluttered, low density as minimalist. Color palette: a defined set of colors used to maintain consistency and create harmony. These are the vocabulary a designer uses to critique and justify layout decisions objectively rather than by taste.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, The Principle of Common Region (Gestalt)
text:
## Common region

Items within a boundary are perceived as a group and assumed to share some common characteristic or functionality. Elements placed inside a shared boundary, created by a border, a background color, or strategic whitespace, are automatically understood as related.

## How to use it

Background colors or borders organize interface sections (headers, footers, navigation) and separate controls from content. Visible boundaries clarify relationships: card layouts group an image with its title and rating; tabs and accordions connect a label to its content. Common region is powerful enough to override other grouping cues such as proximity or similarity, so it is especially useful in complex layouts.

## Anti-pattern: overuse

Excessive borders and colored boxes add visual clutter without benefit. Before adding a container, ask whether proximity and whitespace alone would suffice. Overusing boxes can create false floors that discourage users from scrolling past what looks like the end of the content.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Aesthetic and Minimalist Design (Usability Heuristic 8)
text:
## Aesthetic and minimalist design (Heuristic 8)

Interfaces should not contain information which is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information in an interface competes with the relevant units of information and diminishes their relative visibility.

## Core ideas

Information competition: unnecessary elements actively harm usability by obscuring necessary ones; when users cannot find essential features amid clutter, those features effectively do not exist for them. Signal vs noise: maximize signal (high-value elements like clear labels and helper text) and minimize noise (low-resolution or cluttered images, irrelevant information, purely decorative elements). Minimalist does not mean sparse: minimalism here means limiting noise to emphasize necessary information; a good design contains all the elements a user's task needs, neither too few nor too many. Aesthetics matter for first impressions and brand, but clarity always supersedes visual flourish.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, The Characteristics of Minimalism in Web Design
text:
## Characteristics of minimalism

From an analysis of 112 minimalist websites, the defining characteristics (present in at least 75 percent of sampled sites) are: Flat patterns and textures (96 percent): removing highlights, shadows, gradients, and other textures that make elements look glossy or three-dimensional. Limited or monochromatic color palette (95 percent): nearly half used exclusively monochromatic schemes and 46 percent used one or two accent colors, using color strategically to create interest or direct attention without adding graphics. Restricted features and elements (87 percent): eliminate anything not required to support the core functionality or message. Maximized negative space (84 percent): empty areas direct attention and aid comprehension, balanced against content visibility and accessibility. Dramatic typography (75 percent): bold type communicates meaning and establishes hierarchy when few elements remain.

## Non-defining trends

Grid layouts (43 percent), large background images or video (57 percent), circular elements (16 percent), and hidden navigation (13 percent) appear often but are not core to minimalism. Hidden navigation in particular can hurt discoverability, a caution against equating minimalism with hiding functionality.

title: Interaction Design Foundation, Gestalt Principles
text:
## Gestalt principles

Gestalt principles describe how humans perceive visual elements as unified wholes rather than isolated parts. As Kurt Koffka put it, the whole is other than the sum of the parts. The mind organizes sensory information into meaningful groups, enabling rapid comprehension.

## Core principles

Proximity: elements close together are perceived as a single group, separate from distant elements. Similarity: items that share visual characteristics (color, shape, size) are grouped together. Closure: humans fill gaps to perceive complete shapes, which lets logos like the WWF panda work with incomplete forms. Symmetry and order: symmetrically arranged elements appear grouped and organized, which grid systems implement for balanced layouts. Common fate: elements moving in the same direction are perceived as a group; directional cues like arrows suggest related functionality. Continuity: the eye follows smooth paths and curves, preferring continuous flow. Figure-ground: foreground elements stand out from the background, and strong text-to-background contrast guides attention and reduces cognitive load. Pragnanz (law of simplicity): humans simplify complex visual information, preferring basic geometric shapes, which justifies rectangles and circles in interface design.

title: Interaction Design Foundation, Color Theory
text:
## Color theory

The color wheel, invented by Isaac Newton in 1666, organizes color, understood as human perception of wavelengths of light, into primary (red, blue, yellow), secondary (mixes of primaries), and tertiary (mixes of a primary and a secondary).

## Color properties

Hue: the attribute that distinguishes one color (red, blue, green) from another. Saturation: the purity and vividness of a color, from fully saturated (vibrant) to desaturated (grayed). Value: a color's relative lightness or darkness, crucial for creating contrast and depth.

## Color harmonies

Monochromatic: one hue with varied shades and tints, for minimal cohesive designs. Analogous: three adjacent colors on the wheel, for natural harmony. Complementary: opposite pairs (blue and yellow) to maximize contrast. Split-complementary: a complementary pair plus the colors on either side of one, to soften intensity. Triadic: three colors equally spaced 120 degrees apart, vibrant and high contrast. Tetradic or square: four colors (two complementary pairs or 90 degree spacing) that need careful balance.

## Color temperature

Warm colors (yellow, orange, red) suggest passion, energy, and happiness; cool colors (green, blue, purple) convey calm and soothing impressions; neutrals (gray, brown, white, black) carry no inherent emotion and are the workhorses of an interface, letting one or two accent colors do the signaling.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Low-Contrast Text Is Not the Answer
text:
## Anti-pattern: low-contrast text

The trend of light-grey text on a white background stems from a misapplication of minimalism: designers lower contrast to keep an interface looking minimal while packing in dense content. It causes real harm.

## Why it hurts

Legibility suffers and people are less trusting of text that is hard to read. Discoverability drops because faint elements are missed during scanning. User confidence falls, as users blame themselves and abandon the site. Mobile is worse, because low-contrast text is nearly impossible to read under screen glare. It creates accessibility barriers for the millions of users with presbyopia, macular degeneration, glaucoma, and cataracts. It increases cognitive strain, because dimmed text mimics the convention that disabled or unavailable features are greyed out, sending a false signal.

## The standard and the fix

The article references W3C's Contrast (Minimum), Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3. The fix is not to lower contrast: instead reduce information density, adjust font sizing, check colors against accessibility standards, reposition elements, or use expandable accordions.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, F-Shaped Pattern of Reading Web Content
text:
## The F-shaped reading pattern

Eye-tracking shows users often scan text-heavy pages in an F shape: a horizontal sweep across the top, a shorter horizontal scan partway down, and a vertical descent down the left side of the content.

## Implications for layout

First lines of text on a page receive more gazes than subsequent lines, and words at the beginning of a line get more attention than words toward the right. So crucial information placed far right or buried deep in a paragraph is systematically overlooked. Put the most important words first, front-load headings and the opening sentences of paragraphs, and place key content along the top and left.

## It is a symptom, not a goal

The F-pattern is the default only when there are no strong cues to attract the eyes toward meaningful information: it appears when text is unformatted, users want efficiency, and motivation is low. Good formatting counteracts it: headings, bolded keywords, bulleted lists, concise opening paragraphs, and visual grouping pull users toward important content instead of leaving them to fixate on the left margin.
